newsitem.title: UK: UK companies reach dog lovers, others on Internet - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK companies reach dog lovers, others on Internet - survey.

text.p: British companies have jumped onto the Internet to sell their products, search for new business, recruit staff and entertain consumers, according to a Reuters survey on Monday.

Eighty percent of Britain's top 50 advertisers have created "home pages" on the World Wide Web, the part of the Internet where users click with a mouse and move from one graphics-linked page to another.
Nearly half of the companies that responded to a survey, "Advertising and Marketing on the Internet," said they also advertised on or sponsored Web sites other than their own.
Some Web sites help consumers shop from home, like Waterstone's Bookstores, where you can search for and order books.
Others offer consumers advise, like, a Web site run by Pedigree Petfoods, a part of Mars consumer group.
The Waltham.com Web site offers dog lovers advice about pet care, including how to choose the right dog.
There are now an estimated 3.6 million Internet users in Britain, and the number is growing exponentially, according to NOP Research Group Ltd.
Asda supermarket chain told Reuters it reshaped its recruitment strategy by setting up part of its Web site for young people seeking jobs.
B & Q, a British chain of home-improvement stores, offers Internet users advice on how to install a shower, build a patio, fit electric sockets and fulfil other tasks at home on its Web site.
"(The Internet) is not a mass-market medium, but it's moving very fast," said John Hosking, a marketing manager at Guinness.
He said Guinness was pleasantly surprised some 70,000 Internet users downloaded onto their computers a Guinness screen saver -- an image that decorates a computer screen not actively in use.
"It was a graphic way of saying how powerful the Internet is. People who are hooked up to the Internet are driving it hard," he said.
While several British companies said they were using the Internet to communicate with the mostly young people who surf cyberspace, some said they were targetting older people as well.
